comments.author: @Hector-bj3ls
comments.text:
I don't think it comes up with stuff that we couldn't come up with. I think it just has a less biased view of the search space. 

Humans form opinions on things and steer themselves away from certain choices because they "already know it won't work". The AI works more like the ideal scientist. It just tries the thing that seems most probably according to all the data it has available. Even if that seems like it "obviously wouldn't work".

Actually, that might explain hallucinations. Because some things that obviously won't work also literally don't work.

Which is why you need to keep all opinions in equal parts in your training data (for LLMs) because otherwise it'll do what humans do. Form opinions that make no sense because it doesn't have all the counter data available.

comments.author: @NetTubeUser
comments.text: 10:56 -- I don't know how your brain works, but I can tell you that your analysis and perspective, are wrong. You don't think in 3D correctly. The perceived leaning of the robot is due to the camera angle or perspective. If the camera is not taking a front shot at zero degrees but rather at an angle (like 15 degrees upward), it can create an optical illusion making the robot appear as if it’s leaning. This is a common phenomenon in photography known as "perspective distortion," where the camera's viewpoint can distort the perceived dimensions and positions of objects in the photo. So, the robot is standing straight and the perceived leaning is due to the camera angle. Consequently, there is nothing wrong with this robot, and it stands perfectly straight on the ground.

comments.author: @Urgelt
comments.text:
The physical aspects of robotics are trivial.

The magic is in the AI. That is where previous humanoid robots have failed - they are stuck with hard-coded demonstrations.

The Tesla community - folks who follow they're progress closely - are naturally interested in Optimus. It gets discussed. Alas, not much is in the public eye about AI in Optimus.

Elon Musk has dropped a hint or two. He suggested that humanoid robots can use most of what the company already has developed for FSD.

So FSD is worth a look.

FSD is not an LLM. It is centered around real-time video feeds. Weights trained on video data centrally are distributed to cars, which are equipped with custom neural net chips. These chips process real-time video feeds from multiple cameras, create a virtual real-time simulation of the cars' environs, make predictions, and navigate cars through the real world through controllers. As of V.12, which hasn't yet been released outside of the company, the entire software stack is AI. No hard-coding.

It works pretty well. They're chasing corner cases.

One of the tricks Tesla has is auto-labeling onjects. They used to employ over a thousand human labelers. Most of those jobs are gone.

In its current state, FSD has very little of the multi-modal functionality of an LLM. The underlying model was conceived in about 2018. Training is brute force - millions upon millions of miles of training data, vast amounts of compute.

LLMs appear, to my eye, to represent an advance in training efficiency over FSD. And Tesla's training compute capability is visual, not multi-modal. I am wondering if the model is... Obsolete. Overcome by events. I can't begin to guess how it might be affected by LLM progress. Some sort of melding? Total replacement?

Can an LLM operate a car automomously?

Not in the current generation. Not enough progress on video, not real-time enough.

But I have the feeling that advances in LLMs will require a course change of some sort at Tesla affecting both FSD and Optimus.

It will be a fascinating topic to track!
